title: two flames, eighteen minutes before sunset
hookLine: Friday afternoon, a match, two flames, and hands over the eyes
tomorrow: you already speak a little Yiddish

cards: Friday afternoon, and the clock is running. The oven's on, someone's still in the shower, a kid can't find their shoes.
Then, at a minute printed on a calendar on the fridge, someone strikes a match and lights two candles. They circle their hands over the flames, cover their eyes, and whisper a blessing.
When they look up, the week is over.

teach.b: This is how Shabbat begins: the day of rest, from Friday sunset until the stars come out on Saturday night. Why sunset? In the Torah's first chapter, each day closes the same way: there was evening and there was morning.

Evening comes first, so a day starts in the dark. And since lighting a fire is one of the kinds of work that stop on Shabbat, the candles go on while it's still light, in many towns eighteen minutes early, as a margin.
The rest day is commanded twice, in two wordings: remember the day, and observe it. Zachor and shamor. One flame for each.
Then the hands over the eyes. Usually you say a blessing and then do the thing. But once this blessing is said, Shabbat has begun, and no new fire can be lit.
So people light first, cover their eyes, bless, and then look, as if the light were new. And why light at all?
The rabbis said it's for shalom bayit, peace in the home: a light so the family can see each other's faces at dinner.

how: On Friday before sunset, many Jewish homes light two Shabbat candles (some add one for each child); the one lighting circles their hands over the flames, covers their eyes and says the blessing, then greets the family with Shabbat shalom.

games.q: what's inside the flames — tap the pairs.

s: it starts at sunset on Friday: there was evening, and there was morning.
people cover their eyes because they light before the blessing
once the blessing is said, Shabbat has begun. so: light, cover, bless, look.
the two candles stand for the two tablets
the usual answer is remember and observe, the two wordings of the rest day.

games.q: it's Shabbat and Hanukkah at once, and you can afford only one light. which do the rabbis say to buy?
o: the Hanukkah light, because it's rarer.
the Shabbat light, for peace in the home.
games.why: the Shabbat light, for shalom bayit, peace in the home: a light so the family can see each other at the table.

practice: One breath with the bell. Look at the nearest light: a lamp, a window, even this screen. Breathe in.
Close your eyes, the way people do after lighting. As you breathe out, open them slowly, as if the light were new.

wordCard.voice: The candles. Two flames before sunset on Friday: remember, and observe. Second word.

orig.note: Hebrew: lights, candles. the blessing speaks of the ner shel Shabbat, the Shabbat light.

carryVoice: Your line: light, then rest. First the flame, then the week can stop. That's day two.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 23b (the Shabbat lamp before the Hanukkah lamp, for peace in the home)
Mishnah Shabbat 7:2 (kindling among the kinds of work)
